stem:
A fictional mining and farming district in Zimbabwe has seven towns, A to G, joined by eight tarred roads: A–B, A–C, A–D, A–E, B–C, D–E, E–F and F–G. Town A is the district's main commercial centre. A chrome mine near town G sends ore to a port about 900 km away.

Table 1 gives distances between two of the towns (fictional data).

| Route | Straight-line distance (km) | Distance by road (km) |
|---|---|---|
| Town A to town G | 120 | 156 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which mode of transport is most suitable for carrying the chrome ore from the mine to the port?

options.rationale: Correct: chrome ore is heavy and bulky and travels a long distance, which rail handles cheaply.
Air freight is far too expensive for bulky, low-value ore.
Pipelines carry only liquids and gases.
Bicycles carry tiny loads over short distances.

parts.explanation: Bulky, low-value goods over long distances suit rail.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the beta index of the district's road network. Give your answer to two decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What does your answer to (b) show about the network?

options.content: It is a simple branching network with no circuits
options.rationale: That would need a beta index below 1.

options.content: It has circuits, so some towns have alternative routes
options.rationale: Correct: a beta index above 1 means there are more links than nodes, so circuits exist.

options.content: Every town is directly joined to every other town
options.rationale: That would need far more links; G, for example, is joined only to F.

options.content: The roads are much longer than straight lines
options.rationale: Route length is measured by the detour index, not the beta index.

parts.explanation: β above 1 indicates a connected network with circuits (here A–B–C and A–D–E).

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Use Table 1 to calculate the detour index for the road from town A to town G.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why town A has become the district's main commercial centre.

points.description: Town A has the most links (four roads), so it is the most accessible town in the network.
People and goods from many towns can reach A directly, so shops, banks and services locate there to serve the largest market.
Its position at the junction attracts transport services (bus ranks, depots), which brings more trade (cumulative growth).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Town A is joined directly to four other towns, more than any other, so it is the easiest place to reach. Shops, banks and wholesalers set up there to serve customers from the whole district, and bus ranks and depots at the junction bring even more trade.

parts.explanation: Accessibility at a network junction encourages commercial growth.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe Zimbabwe's main road and rail links to seaports in neighbouring countries.

points.description: The Beira corridor: road and rail from Harare through Mutare (Forbes border post) to Beira in Mozambique, with the fuel pipeline to Feruka.
Road and rail south through Beitbridge across the Limpopo to South Africa and its ports such as Durban.
A railway from the south-east of Zimbabwe to Maputo in Mozambique.
Routes north and west through Chirundu or Victoria Falls into Zambia (and onward to Dar es Salaam), or via Plumtree into Botswana.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The shortest route is the Beira corridor, with road and rail running from Harare through Mutare to Beira, beside the fuel pipeline. Road and rail also run south via Beitbridge to the South African ports such as Durban. A railway links the south-east to Maputo, and routes through Chirundu and Victoria Falls lead to Zambia and on towards Dar es Salaam.

parts.explanation: Name the route, the modes and the port.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of road and rail for a Zimbabwean exporter.

points.description: Road advantage: door-to-door delivery and flexible timing, reaching places without railway sidings.
Road disadvantage: higher cost per tonne over long distances; small loads per lorry; delays and damage on poor roads.
Rail advantage: carries large, bulky loads cheaply over long distances (for example coal, chrome, fertiliser).
Rail disadvantage: fixed routes and timetables, so goods need transfers by lorry; shortages of locomotives and wagons cause delays.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Road is flexible: a lorry collects from the farm or factory and delivers to the customer when needed, but it carries small loads and costs more per tonne over long distances, and poor roads cause delays. Rail moves large tonnages of bulky goods such as chrome cheaply over long distances, but it runs only on fixed lines and timetables, so goods must be transferred, and a shortage of working wagons can cause delays. Road therefore suits small, urgent or short-distance consignments, and rail suits bulky goods over long distances.

parts.explanation: A comparison should balance both modes and end with which suits which cargo.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: With reference to Zimbabwe, explain the transport problems that affect the movement of goods and evaluate the solutions that have been or could be used.

points.description: Landlocked position: long distances to the ports of Beira, Maputo and Durban add cost and time.
Border delays: long queues of lorries at busy posts such as Beitbridge.
Poor road condition: potholes, narrow roads, accidents; overloaded lorries damage roads.
Rail problems: old locomotives and wagons, slow services, freight shifted to road.
Solution evaluated: one-stop border posts and electronic pre-clearance (Chirundu with Zambia) cut waiting times at relatively low cost.
Solution evaluated: rehabilitation and dualisation of main roads funded by tolls are effective but expensive and need maintenance.
Solution evaluated: investment in rolling stock and track would move bulky freight back to rail and protect roads; using several corridors reduces dependence on one route.
Judgement: a combination is needed; a reasoned priority (for example rail plus border efficiency) for a landlocked country.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Because Zimbabwe is landlocked, its exports and imports travel hundreds of kilometres to Beira, Maputo or Durban, which adds cost. Lorries can wait a long time at Beitbridge, the busiest border post. Many roads are narrow and potholed, accidents are common and overloaded lorries make the damage worse. The railway has too few working locomotives and wagons, so bulky goods such as chrome and coal have moved to road, increasing road damage. Several solutions have been tried. One-stop border posts, such as Chirundu with Zambia, let officials of both countries clear lorries once, cutting delays cheaply. Rehabilitating and dualising highways, partly funded by tolls, makes journeys safer and faster, but it is very expensive and roads must be maintained. Recapitalising the railway would take heavy freight off the roads and lower costs per tonne, but needs large investment. Using the Beira, Beitbridge and Maputo routes keeps trade moving if one corridor is blocked. No single solution is enough; faster border clearance combined with a stronger railway would do most to cut the cost of trade for a landlocked country.

parts.explanation: Explain several problems with Zimbabwean detail, then weigh up solutions and reach a judgement.

explanation: A ZIMSEC Paper 2 Section C transport question: mode choice, beta and detour indices, accessibility, routes to the sea, comparing modes and an extended evaluation of transport problems.
hints: Count each town as a node and each road between two towns as a link.
Detour index = road distance ÷ straight-line distance × 100.
